name: Amazon
summary: Practice array, cache, and frequency-ranking problems common in Amazon-style interview prep.

questions.title: Two Sum Product Pair
questions.summary: Find two input positions whose values add to a target.
questions.prompt: Given a list of integers and a target, return the indices of two numbers whose sum equals the target.
constraints: Do not reuse the same element twice.

diagrams.title: Complement lookup
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Read value] --> B[Need target - value]
  B --> C{Seen?}
  C -->|yes| D[Return pair]
  C -->|no| E[Store index]

solutionTracks.title: One Pass Complement Map
solutionTracks.summary: Scan once while remembering earlier values by value so each new item can close a pair immediately.

steps.title: Store earlier values
steps.explanation: Keep a map from each number already scanned to its index, because only earlier positions can pair with the current position.

steps.title: Ask for the complement
steps.explanation: For each value, compute target minus value and check whether that complement was seen before.

steps.title: Return the pair
steps.explanation: When the complement exists, the stored index and current index form a valid answer without more scanning.

solutionTracks.explanation: The invariant is that the map contains every candidate from the prefix before the current index. If a valid pair ends at the current item, its partner must already be in that prefix, so the lookup is sufficient.

solutionTracks.title: Sorted Value Pairs
solutionTracks.summary: Sort values with their original indexes, then move two pointers inward until the target sum appears.

steps.title: Preserve indexes
steps.explanation: Pair every value with its original index before sorting so the final answer still uses input positions.

steps.title: Use sorted direction
steps.explanation: If the current sum is too small move the left pointer right; if too large move the right pointer left.

steps.title: Return original positions
steps.explanation: When the sum equals the target, return the stored original indexes rather than the sorted positions.

solutionTracks.explanation: Sorting creates monotonic movement: increasing the left pointer raises the sum and decreasing the right pointer lowers it. That means every discarded pair cannot become valid later.

questions.title: LRU Cache
questions.summary: Implement a fixed-capacity cache that evicts the least recently used key.
questions.prompt: Design a cache with get and put operations. Both should update recency, and the cache should evict the least recently used key when capacity is exceeded.

examples.explanation: Key 2 is evicted because key 1 was recently read.

constraints: Aim for constant-time get and put in the main solution.

diagrams.title: LRU structure
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  M[Hash map key to node] --> N[Doubly linked list]
  O[Oldest] --> A[Node]
  A --> B[Newest]

solutionTracks.title: Hash Map Plus Recency List
solutionTracks.summary: Combine O(1) key lookup with a doubly linked list that keeps least-recently-used entries at one end.

steps.title: Separate lookup and recency
steps.explanation: Use a map for key to node lookup and a list for oldest to newest ordering.

steps.title: Refresh on access
steps.explanation: Every get or update moves the node to the newest end because it was just used.

steps.title: Evict from the old end
steps.explanation: When capacity is exceeded, remove the node next to the oldest sentinel and delete its key from the map.

solutionTracks.explanation: The map answers where a key lives and the list answers which key is oldest. Updating both structures together preserves O(1) operations and correct eviction order.

solutionTracks.title: Timestamped Map For Small Capacity
solutionTracks.summary: Store last-used timestamps with each key and scan for the oldest key only when eviction is needed.

steps.title: Store value and time
steps.explanation: Each get or put increments a clock and writes that clock as the key last-used time.

steps.title: Use map lookups
steps.explanation: Reads still find keys in O(1), so missing and present keys are straightforward.

steps.title: Scan on eviction
steps.explanation: If the cache grows past capacity, scan the entries and remove the smallest timestamp.

solutionTracks.explanation: This version is simpler and can be accepted for small capacities or as a stepping stone. It preserves the same recency semantics but spends more time during eviction.

questions.title: Top K Frequent Items
questions.summary: Return the k values that appear most frequently in an input array.
questions.prompt: Given an integer array and an integer k, return any ordering of the k most frequent values.
constraints: Any order is acceptable unless the prompt adds a tie-breaker.

solutionTracks.title: Frequency Count With Min Heap
solutionTracks.summary: Count values, keep only the k largest frequencies in a min heap, and return the heap contents.

steps.title: Count first
steps.explanation: A hash map converts the input into value to frequency counts.

steps.title: Keep heap small
steps.explanation: Push each pair into a min heap and pop when the heap grows beyond k.

steps.title: Read the survivors
steps.explanation: The heap contains the k values whose frequencies survived every smaller-frequency eviction.

solutionTracks.explanation: The min heap always removes the least frequent value among the candidates it has seen. After all counts are processed, only the k strongest candidates remain.

solutionTracks.title: Frequency Buckets
solutionTracks.summary: Group values by frequency, then walk buckets from highest frequency down until k values are collected.

steps.title: Count frequencies
steps.explanation: The highest possible frequency is the length of the input, so frequencies can address an array of buckets.

steps.title: Bucket values
steps.explanation: Append each distinct value into the bucket that matches its count.

steps.title: Walk backward
steps.explanation: Visit frequencies from high to low and collect values until the answer has k entries.

solutionTracks.explanation: Bucket indexes are already sorted by frequency, so no comparison sort is necessary. Walking backward visits values in non-increasing frequency order.
